title: Why TSMC Is Building Memory Above Processor Logic
gist: TSMC demonstrated at the 2025 VLSI Symposium a 1T1C oxide-semiconductor memory built in the back-end-of-line above processor logic, as a denser cache alternative to SRAM (0.75 V, under 8 ns cycles, over 128 ms retention at 85 C). The post stresses these are research results, not proof of production readiness or of a move into commodity DRAM.

insights.claim: TSMC's BEOL memory research embeds memory cells in the interconnect layers above a processor's logic rather than manufacturing memory solely as separate chips, positioned as a denser alternative to SRAM for cache.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Stacking cache above logic could change the cache density versus area trade-off in advanced processors.
insights.quote: embeds memory cells within the interconnect layers above a processor’s logic circuitry

insights.claim: The design uses one transistor and one capacitor per cell, with an oxide-semiconductor transistor and a capacitor made by a low-temperature process.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Low-temperature BEOL-compatible processing is what allows stacking above finished logic.
insights.locator: The design uses one transistor and one capacitor

insights.claim: TSMC's paper reports operation at 0.75 volts, random memory cycles below eight nanoseconds, and data retention exceeding 128 milliseconds at 85 degrees C.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Benchmark specs for the demonstrated cell; retention is DRAM-like and implies refresh.

insights.claim: These are encouraging research results that do not establish readiness for commercial production.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Cautions against reading the demonstration as a product roadmap.
insights.quote: they do not establish readiness for commercial production

insights.claim: Placing memory above logic could let designers spread storage over the processor's available area and potentially require fewer memory layers for a given capacity, though usable area, wiring, heat and manufacturing constraints decide the real advantage.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Area and thermal limits will determine whether the density benefit is real.
insights.locator: Why does the processor’s footprint matter?

insights.claim: More nearby memory could reduce transfers to external memory, potentially improving performance and energy efficiency for AI processors that need rapid access to enormous data volumes, and denser caches give designers more flexibility balancing compute against storage.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: On-die dense memory could ease the AI memory wall and affect demand for external memory.

insights.claim: Embedded BEOL memory should not be confused with a confirmed move into standalone commodity DRAM; the report reads TSMC's statement reaffirming its foundry focus as leaving room for memory development, which does not confirm a commercial roadmap.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: DRAM makers should not treat this as a confirmed TSMC entry into commodity memory.
insights.locator: However, embedded BEOL memory should not be confused

insights.claim: The key open question is whether TSMC can translate the demonstration into reliable, economical manufacturing at scale while meeting customers' speed, capacity, power and integration requirements.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Manufacturability and cost, not feasibility, are the milestones to watch.
